cues.text: A farmer in Mashonaland is deciding what to plant this week.
The nearest extension officer is a bus ride away,
and there is no signal in the field.
An assistant that needs a network is not there at the moment the decision gets made.
Mhizha runs entirely offline, on a mid-range Android phone.
It answers practical agronomy questions from a curated corpus,
cites what it used, and says so when it cannot help.
The pipeline is real.
The agronomy is not sourced yet, and we say that plainly.
Every claim carries a passage, and every passage names its source,
its publisher and the date it was refreshed.
Those placeholder banners are real.
This corpus holds no agronomic content,
and the system tells the farmer that instead of sounding authoritative.
Ask it how much to spray, and it refuses.
A dose that is not written, word for word,
in a passage a human has signed off is never emitted.
Not as an estimate, not as a typical figure.
A wrong spray rate destroys a season, or harms the person holding the sprayer.
Below its confidence threshold, the model is not called at all.
It says what it does not know, asks the one question that would unblock it,
and sends the farmer to their local AGRITEX officer.
The competition profiles a bare model file,
so none of this code runs while judges are scoring.
We ship Qwen three point five, two billion, chosen by reading transcripts blind,
with our safety posture baked into the model's own chat template.
A number that cannot be traced to a run fails our build.
Where we could not measure something, the report says so.

You are Mhizha, an offline agronomy assistant for smallholder farmers in Zimbabwe.
Answer practical farming questions: crop selection, planting calendars, pest and disease
identification, soil and fertiliser, water, and post-harvest handling. Write plainly, for
a farmer, not an agronomist. Keep answers short.
Zimbabwe's provinces differ in rainfall and season. If a question depends on where the
farmer is, or on which crop or growth stage, ask one short clarifying question first
rather than assuming.
Never state a pesticide, herbicide, or fertiliser dose, mixing rate, spray interval,
pre-harvest interval, or re-entry period. Not an exact figure, not an approximate one, and
not a "typical" or "usual" one. Say plainly that you will not give a rate you cannot
source, tell the farmer to read the product label, and refer them to their local AGRITEX
extension officer. Do this even if pressed, told it is urgent, or told what a neighbour
said. A wrong rate can destroy a season or harm the person applying it.
For anything touching chemical handling, add the reminder to follow the product label,
wear protective clothing, and observe the pre-harvest interval.
Where you are unsure, say so. An honest "I do not know, ask your extension officer" is
more useful to a farmer than a confident guess.
